property_summary: For any caller, C.owner() returns the stored owner address set at construction/transferOwnership (never the zero address unless explicitly set to zero by renounceOwnership); the mutant that always returns address(0) breaks this by returning zero for some caller inputs.

For every caller, the deployed contract's owner() returns the non-zero address that was set at construction (not address(0)); the mutant that forces owner() to always return address(0) violates this for callers when the constructed owner is non-zero.

For any caller, the deployed reference contract's owner() returns the non-zero address set at construction (the deployer), while the mutant returns address(0) for some caller(s), so owner()'s returned value must equal the constructed owner() and not be zero; the mutant breaks this.

For every caller, the reference contract's owner() returns the non-zero owner address set at construction; the mutant that makes owner() always return address(0) will cause owner() to return zero for some (indeed all) callers, violating this rule.

For every caller address, the correct contract's owner() returns the non-zero owner set at construction (address(this) passed in setUp), whereas the mutant that forces owner() to always return address(0) will for some caller(s) return a different (zero) address, breaking equality with the constructed owner.

For any caller address X, calling owner() on the correct contract returns the stored owner (the deployer) and thus is independent of the caller; the mutant returning msg.sender makes owner() equal the caller for some X, violating this invariant.

For all callers, the reference contract's owner() always returns the fixed deployer address (set in constructor), whereas the mutant returns msg.sender causing owner() to sometimes differ from the stored deployer when called by other addresses.

For every caller address, the deployed (reference) contract's owner() returns the same fixed deployer address; the mutant returns the caller (msg.sender) so for some caller addresses the returned owner differs.

For every caller address, the reference contract's owner() always returns the fixed deployer address (the owner stored at construction); the mutant that returns msg.sender will for some caller addresses return a different value, breaking that invariant.

For every caller address, C.owner() returns the same fixed deployer address that was set as the contract owner at construction; the mutant returning msg.sender breaks this because for some callers the returned value will equal the caller rather than the deployer.

For any caller the correct contract's owner() returns the stored _owner (the externally set owner), whereas the mutant returns address(this) instead — so owner() must equal the originally-set owner address for all inputs but the mutant will differ for some.

For any caller/address input, the deployed reference contract's owner() returns the originally set owner address (the value passed to the constructor) while the mutant returns address(this), so owner() == constructor owner for all inputs in the reference but differs for some inputs in the mutant.

For every caller, the reference contract's owner() returns the address supplied as the constructor _operator (the stored owner), whereas the mutant returns address(this) instead — so the property is: owner() == constructor-set owner for all inputs; the mutant violates this for callers when constructor-set owner != address(c).

For all inputs the reference contract's public owner() getter returns the owner address set by the constructor (the stored _owner); the mutant returns address(this) instead, so for any fuzzed owner input not equal to address(c) the mutant's owner() differs and the property is violated.

For all addresses passed as the constructor owner, the reference contract's owner() returns that exact address; the mutant returns address(this) instead, so for some constructor owner inputs (those not equal to address(c)) the mutant's owner() value differs and will break an assertion that owner() == constructorOwner.

For every input (no preconditions), the genuine contract's owner() returns the exact stored owner address; the mutant returns a different address (stored owner + 1) for at least some stored owner values, so calling owner() yields a different returned address and thus violates the equality property.

For any stored owner address, calling owner() returns that exact stored owner; the mutant adds 1 to the stored owner (as uint160) so for some stored owner values the returned address differs and thus breaks the equality property.

The contract's owner() getter always returns the stored owner address; the mutant shifts the stored owner by +1 (as uint160) so for some stored owner values owner() will return a different address and violate that equality.

For every possible stored owner address, the deployed contract's owner() view must return that exact stored owner; the mutant adds 1 to the stored owner (as uint160) so for some stored owner values owner() will return a different address, violating equality.

For every stored owner value, C.owner() returns that exact stored owner address (the reference preserves the stored owner); the mutant returns address(uint160(_owner)+1) so for some stored owner values the returned address differs, violating equality.

Invariant: calling transferOwnership(newOwner) as the current owner always allows transferring ownership to the provided newOwner (even if newOwner is zero) in the reference; the mutant tightens the check to re-check caller and can break transferring to the zero address for some fuzzed newOwner values (e.g. address(0)).

Reference contract allows the owner to transfer ownership to any address (including address(0)) when called by the current owner; the mutant additionally (and redundantly) requires owner() == _msgSender() again and so can behave identically for owner calls but will block non-owner callers — the general rule: only the current owner can successfully call transferOwnership; the mutant tightens checks causing some calls (from non-owner but privileged contexts) to revert, so there exist inputs (a fuzzed caller address) where reference allows the call to succeed but mutant rejects it.

For any caller address x and any newOwner address y, in the reference contract a call to transferOwnership(y) succeeds iff the caller is the current owner (i.e. only owner can transfer); the mutant inserts an extra redundant require that rechecks owner()==_msgSender() and thus can cause some calls that would succeed in the reference (when called via a contract that forwards calls preserving msg.sender semantics) to revert—so there exists a fuzzed caller (a forwarding contract) that makes the mutant revert while the reference still succeeds.

For any caller contract F that forwards a call so msg.sender seen by C is F (i.e. F calls C.transferOwnership), the reference allows the current owner (the original deployer) to transfer ownership to any newOwner when F forwards the call, but the mutant's extra require can cause the forwarded call to revert for some forwarding caller (the fuzzer can find such a forwarding caller address), so there exist inputs where reference succeeds and mutant fails.

For any caller address A and target newOwner N, when A is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(N) must succeed (reference allows transferring to any address including address(0)); the mutant can cause the call to revert for some caller setups (e.g. a forwarding contract that does not preserve msg.sender semantics), so there exist fuzzed caller addresses that make the mutant fail while the reference still succeeds.

Invariant: transferOwnership(newOwner) called by the current owner never allows setting owner to the zero address (owner() != address(0)) in the reference; the mutant that removes the zero-address check permits transferOwnership(address(0)) and thus can make owner() == address(0) for some input.

For any caller that is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) never results in owner() being the zero address in the reference implementation; the mutant that removes the zero-address check can make owner() == address(0) when newOwner is address(0).

For any caller that is the current owner and any address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract never results in owner() == address(0) (it forbids transferring ownership to the zero address); the mutant that removes the zero-address check can make owner() == address(0) for some fuzzed newOwner input (newOwner == address(0)).

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) on the correct contract never sets owner() to the zero address (it rejects newOwner==address(0)); the mutant that removes that check can make owner()==address(0) for some fuzzed newOwner input.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) never results in owner() being the zero address in the reference contract (it rejects newOwner == address(0)); the mutant that removed that check can make owner() == address(0) for some fuzzed newOwner input, so owner() == address(0) can be observed after the call.

For any caller address newOwner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) by the current owner always updates c.owner() to newOwner (reference preserves ownership transfer); the mutant's modified onlyOwner prevents the legitimate owner call from succeeding for some callers, so there exist inputs where transferOwnership does not update owner.

For any address newOwner and caller equal to the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and updates owner() to newOwner; the mutant's changed onlyOwner check with a hardcoded address(0) causes some legitimate owner calls to not update owner() (failing for at least some newOwner inputs).

For any caller that is the current owner and any candidate newOwner address, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always updates owner() to newOwner in the reference; the mutant's onlyOwner change prevents some legitimate owner calls from succeeding, so there exist fuzzed newOwner values where owner() is not updated.

For any caller who is the current owner, calling transferOwnership(newOwner) always succeeds and updates owner() to newOwner in the reference; the mutant's onlyOwner modifier (which checks for address(0) instead of owner()) causes some owner-invocations to be blocked, so there exist fuzzed newOwner addresses for which transferOwnership does not update owner().

For any caller that is the current owner and any candidate newOwner (fuzzed), calling transferOwnership(newOwner) succeeds and updates owner() to newOwner in the reference; the mutant's modified onlyOwner (which compares _msgSender() to address(0) instead of owner()) causes some legitimate owner calls to be blocked, so there exist fuzzed newOwner values for which transferOwnership does not update owner().

For all callers, only the contract owner can change operator via setOperator (i.e. calls to setOperator by non-owners do not change c.operator()); the mutant removes the onlyOwner guard so some non-owner caller can change operator and thus violate this property.

For all callers, only the contract owner can change operator via setOperator (i.e., after any call to setOperator by a non-owner, operator remains unchanged); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so a non-owner call can change operator and violate this rule.

Invariant: Only the contract owner is allowed to change operator — i.e., any call to setOperator made by an address that is not the owner must NOT modify c.operator(); the mutant (removing onlyOwner) allows a non-owner caller to change operator, violating this rule for some caller addresses.

For every caller who is not the contract owner, calling setOperator must NOT change c.operator() (reference enforces this via onlyOwner); the mutant removes the onlyOwner check so some non-owner caller can change operator, violating this rule.

For any caller address, only the contract owner can successfully change the operator via setOperator (i.e., a non-owner call must not update operator); the mutant removes the onlyOwner guard so some non-owner call will change operator, violating this rule.

For any caller and any input _operator, calling setOperator on the reference contract sets operator to the provided _operator (i.e. operator() == _operator after the call); the mutant instead sets operator = tx.origin so there exist inputs where operator() != _operator and the property fails.

For every external caller and any address _operator, calling setOperator(_operator) on the correct contract sets operator() == _operator; the mutant instead sets operator = tx.origin, so for some calls (when msg.sender != tx.origin) operator() != _operator and the property is violated.

For every caller and any _operator value, calling setOperator(_operator) on the correct contract sets operator() equal to the caller-supplied _operator (operator == _operator); the mutant instead sets operator = tx.origin so there exist calls (when msg.sender != tx.origin) where operator() != _operator.

For any caller and any _operator address, calling setOperator(_operator) results in c.operator() equaling the provided _operator on the reference; the mutant sets operator = tx.origin instead, so when msg.sender != tx.origin the mutant will make c.operator() != _operator.

For any caller X and any address newOp, when X (msg.sender) calls setOperator(newOp) on the correct contract, operator() is set to newOp; the mutant instead sets operator to tx.origin, so if msg.sender != tx.origin the mutant yields operator() != newOp (the fuzzer will supply a contract caller to make msg.sender != tx.origin).

For any caller addr, calling setOperator(newOperator) succeeds if and only if msg.sender == owner() in the reference; the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin instead of msg.sender allows a contract caller (via delegatecall context differences) to bypass the owner check and change operator when tx.origin matches owner, so the invariant 'non-owner contract callers cannot change operator' is violated by the mutant for some inputs.

Any direct calls to setOperator by a non-owner EOA must not change operator in the reference contract; the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin instead of msg.sender can be made to change operator when a contract call via delegatecall causes tx.origin to equal owner, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For any caller address X and new operator address Y, in the correct contract only the owner (owner() == msg.sender) can successfully change operator via setOperator(Y); the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin instead of msg.sender allows a contract to change operator when tx.origin == owner (via a delegatecall bridge), so there exist inputs (an owner EOAs address used as tx.origin and a bridge contract caller) that make the mutant permit the change while the reference forbids it.

For all caller addresses and proposed operator addresses, only EOAs that are the contract owner (msg.sender == owner()) can successfully change operator via setOperator; the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin instead of msg.sender allows a non-owner contract caller (with tx.origin == owner) to change operator, violating this invariant for some inputs.

For all callers and proposed operator addresses, only a direct call from the owner (msg.sender == owner()) can change operator; the mutant that compares owner() to tx.origin allows a non-owner contract caller (with tx.origin == owner) to change operator, violating this rule for some inputs.

For every input address, the reference contract allows the owner to set rewardsRecipient to any address (including the zero address), while the mutant erroneously rejects the zero address causing calls that set rewardsRecipient to address(0) to revert (i.e. the reference accepts zero address assignments but the mutant sometimes does not).

For any address x and owner caller, the reference contract accepts setRewardsRecipient(x) (succeeds) and then rewardsRecipient() == x; the mutant rejects x == address(0) (reverting) so there exists an x (the zero address) for which the mutant breaks this rule.
